newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan polls forecast LDP win, but caution remains.
newsitem.headline: Japan polls forecast LDP win, but caution remains.

text.p: Japan's big newspapers on Wednesday forecast outright victory for Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in Sunday's general elections, but politicians on all sides said the contest was still too close to call.

Voter surveys at the weekend showed Hashimoto's conservative Liberal Democratic Party was likely to win 251 seats -- a simple majority in the 500-seat Lower House of parliament -- while its main rival Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) would lose seats, the liberal daily Asahi Shimbun said.

Conservative dailies Yomiuri Shimbun and Sankei Shimbun, and the moderate Mainichi Shimbun, reported similar survey results, reinforcing a trend in which the LDP's well-oiled machine has gained strength during the 12-day campaign.

The Asahi cautioned, however, that more than half the voters it surveyed had not made up their minds. Pundits said choices made by floating voters -- including abstention -- as well as the weather on election day, were still key variables.

"The surveys are a very crude measure of what could happen -- not least because it appears a lot of voters will not make up their minds until election day," said John Neuffer, a political analyst at Mitsui Marine Research Institute.
Reacting to the rosy projections, LDP Secretary-General Koichi Kato told party support groups not to let down their guard or let turnout fall.
"Staying away from polls thinking the LDP is home safe is tantamount to giving half a vote to the opposition," Kato told supporters at party headquarters.

Shinshinto officials dismissed suggestions that the tide was turning against them, reminding party members that they prevailed against similar odds in last year's elections for the Upper House of parliament.
The LDP's surge draws on its strong lead in the 300 first-past-the-post constituencies, the key component of the new electoral system under which the election is being fought.

The LDP, which ruled Japan unchallenged from 1955-93 then after a brief period out of power came back as the dominant partner in a coalition government from mid-1994, has more than 180 "safe" candidates with strong support bases, Asahi said.
The party was also expected to perform well in the remaining 200 seats contested by proportional representation in 11 regional blocs, it said.

By contrast, Shinshinto, the only opposition party fielding enough candidates to oust the LDP, was in danger of falling below the 160 seats it held when parliament was dissolved last month, the Asahi said.
Shinshinto, another conservative party, was expected to do well in the proportional representation part of the polls, but trailed the LDP in single-seat districts, it said.
All polls said the reformist Democratic Party and the Japan Communist Party were expected to fare well, drawing protest votes from those disillusioned with the mainstream parties.
The biggest losers were expected to be the LDP's coalition partners in the outgoing government, the Social Democratic Party and New Party Sakigake, the surveys said.
